feedback: If a learner keeps the Sun at the base: no sunlight reaches a deep vent — point to exactly where sunlight enters the ENERGY path. If you can't, the producers' energy must be something else. (Some marine snow does drift down, and the oxygen in seawater comes from photosynthesis at the surface, but the vent's PRODUCERS build food using chemical energy, not light.)

If a learner picks the vent's heat as the food energy: heat is not what the bacteria capture to build food. They oxidise a chemical (H2S) and use that chemical energy — line up heat vs chemical energy explicitly.

If a learner says bacteria 'eat' or 'feed on' H2S: just as plants don't eat sunlight, vent bacteria don't eat H2S — they use its chemical energy to synthesise their own food from CO2. Keep CO2 as the carbon source.

If a learner calls it 'photosynthesis in the dark': both processes build food (sugar) from CO2, but the energy input differs — light for photosynthesis, chemical for chemosynthesis. Same kind of food made, fundamentally different fuel (and different by-products: photosynthesis releases oxygen, while H2S oxidation produces sulfur or sulfate).
activities.intendedInsight: Photosynthesis is not the only way to build a food web. Producers do the same job — making food by fixing carbon from CO2 — but can be powered either by light (photosynthesis) or by chemical energy from oxidising H2S (chemosynthesis). Bacteria, not green plants, are the producers at a vent, and the community's energy source is chemical, not the Sun.
learnerActions: First build (or label) a familiar sunlit web: Sun → phytoplankton/plants → consumers, and mark where the energy enters.
Now build a hydrothermal-vent food web set in permanent darkness. Try to place the Sun at the base and notice it cannot power this web — no sunlight reaches kilometres down.

Choose the base's actual energy source from options including 'sunlight', 'the vent's heat', and 'chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S)'. Select the chemical-energy option so chemoautotrophic bacteria become the producers.
Extend the web: bacteria → tube worms / giant clams → vent crabs, and trace the energy flow from the chemical source upward.
Set the two webs side by side and fill a comparison table: inputs, energy source, and product (food/organic matter from CO2) for photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis.
activities.title: Build a vent food web on a different power source

feedback: If a learner treats origin-of-life or alien-life claims as proven: these are reasoned, evidence-based hypotheses still being debated — distinguish what is observed from what is inferred.

If a learner dismisses the moons because 'there's no sunlight': that's the point — vent communities show sunlight isn't required as the energy source, so the relevant question is whether chemical energy, water and minerals are present.
Push for the mechanism of the analogy: name what Earth vents and the moons' suspected environments have in common (chemical energy + water ± minerals) rather than just asserting they are similar.
activities.intendedInsight: Vents reshape the search for life because they show a food web can run on chemical energy and water rather than light. Whether life began at vents, and whether ocean moons host life, are genuine open scientific questions to be argued from evidence and uncertainty — not settled facts.
learnerActions: Take on the question in role: ask and answer 'Why look at hydrothermal vents to search for life beyond Earth?' and 'Could life have begun at vents?'

Set out the reasoning: if life needs chemical energy, water and minerals — which vents supply without sunlight as the energy source — then sunless environments elsewhere are not automatically lifeless.
Apply the analogy to Europa and Enceladus: these icy moons may have subsurface oceans and hydrothermal chemistry but no sunlight; discuss what makes them candidates and what remains unknown.
State explicitly which parts are established (vent communities exist and run without sunlight as their energy source) and which are open hypotheses (origin of life at vents; life on ocean moons).
Weigh at least one piece of evidence for and one source of uncertainty before giving a tentative, reasoned position.
activities.title: Reason with an astrobiologist: did life begin at vents, and where else might it be?

feedback: Producer check: the producers here are bacteria, not plants and not animals — producers need not be green.
Energy vs carbon check: the energy source is chemical (H2S oxidation); the carbon source is CO2. Keep these distinct.
If a learner expects a sunlight input in the energy path: there is none — trace the arrows and confirm the base's energy is chemical, not light.
activities.intendedInsight: A vent community is a complete food web whose base producers are bacteria powered by chemical energy, with no sunlight as the energy source; the same comparison that defines photosynthesis clarifies how chemosynthesis differs.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled vent scene: mineral-rich fluid rising, bacterial mats, tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs — tracing which organism depends on which.
Open a photosynthesis/chemosynthesis comparison showing inputs, energy source and product aligned for each.
Examine an Earth-vent ↔ Europa/Enceladus analogue panel and state what the two settings share.
Answer short checks: name the producer at a vent; name its energy source (oxidising H2S) and its carbon source (CO2); and explain why the community survives with no sunlight as its energy source.
activities.title: Explore and interrogate a vent cross-section

feedback: Gap response (insists the base energy traces to the Sun; claims sunlight seeps down or that drifting detritus feeds the WHOLE community): re-establish chemosynthesis as a genuinely independent energy pathway — the producers' energy is from vent chemicals, not light.

Partial response (says 'chemosynthesis' but can't name H2S oxidation as the energy source or keep CO2 as the carbon source): press for the mechanism — what is oxidised for energy, and where does the carbon come from?
Full response: bacteria oxidise H2S for energy to build food from CO2, cleanly contrasted with photosynthesis, placed at the base of the web, and transferred to astrobiology reasoning.
Asking 'how do the bacteria capture it?' forces the mechanism rather than just the label — require the energy step, not a one-word answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means naming chemosynthesis, identifying the oxidised chemical (H2S) as the energy source, keeping CO2 as the carbon source, and transferring the idea to origin-of-life and ocean-world reasoning — not merely using the word 'chemosynthesis' as a label.
learnerActions: Answer a two-tier diagnostic: given giant tube worms and clams thriving around bacteria in permanent darkness, decide whether sunlight is the energy source the producers capture — and if not, state what is and how the bacteria capture it.

Give the full answer: chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidise H2S (using oxygen dissolved in seawater) for energy and use it to build food from CO2; tube worms, clams and crabs depend on those bacteria; the energy the producers capture is chemical energy from vent fluid (from reactions in the Earth's crust), not sunlight.
Compare a leaf and a vent bacterium: what is the same (both build food from CO2) and what differs (light energy vs chemical energy)?
Predict: if a vent stopped emitting hydrogen sulphide, what happens to the tube worms, and why?
Contrast the two energy sources, identify the vent producer, and reason about how far the Europa/Enceladus analogue holds and what remains unknown.
activities.title: Check and discriminate the concept
